source.how: read-only sysfs on three units running BIOS 5.36_0ACUM027: /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policy*/cpuinfo_max_freq, cpufreq driver and governor
source.note: no workload was run; these are the advertised maxima and the driver's identity

what_it_means: the platform exposes two clusters through one driver. A single-threaded or latency-sensitive job can be pinned to the fast ten (taskset -c 5-9,15-19); that is a supported, reversible placement change, not a clock increase.
what_it_does_not_mean: that the faster cluster is idle-free or that pinning makes a parallel job faster. The DSDT cannot state the ceiling either: its _CPC package carries register descriptors, not values. Nor that pinning doubles anything: capacity-aware scheduling is already in effect.
not_established: whether 3.9 GHz is the silicon maximum
the measured gain of pinning, which needs a benchmark on a unit
the throughput effect of a 2% clock at a fixed workload — the clock moved, the work was not measured

scheduler_capacity.reading: cpu_capacity differs by cluster, so capacity-aware scheduling is active: the scheduler already prefers the fast ten. taskset therefore guarantees placement rather than uncovering it, and the gain for long-running threads is smaller than the clock ratio.

boost_measured.method: one unit: echo 1 > /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/boost, read every policy's cpuinfo_max_freq, then 0 and read again; restored to 0 afterwards
boost_measured.gain: 1.9-2.7% on ten of the twenty CPUs; zero on the other ten
boost_measured.it_is_usable: policy 15's scaling_max_freq followed to the new ceiling and scaling_cur_freq read 3978000, so the cores run at the raised clock while boost is on
boost_measured.reversible: writing 0 restored every ceiling exactly (policy 10-14 to 2808000, 15-19 to 3900000)
